notes: \cpara{Opens, with ``probably,'' on how bad joining a cult is. Even the best case is compared, as a joke, to a failed startup.}

\cpara{Lists the practices of ``real cults'': love bombing, sleep deprivation, isolation, confession, taking all the recruit's money, starvation. No example or source is given. The list serves as a reference point later; sleep deprivation is mentioned eight times in the post.}

\cpara{States the occasion: other people's nervousness that ``they might be joining a cult'' grates on the author's nerves. Later the post says whose question this is: the author is asked it ``a lot more often'' when talking about powerful AIs.}

\cpara{Point one: cultishness is an ``attractor,'' a set of group failures that feed each other, not an essence a group has or lacks. The point, the word ``attractor'' and the entropy image used later are from ``Every Cause Wants to Be a Cult'' (12 December 2007), which said: ``Cultishness is quantitative, not qualitative.''}
\cpara{Contrasts a natural kind: cats and dogs, whose membership is fixed at birth, with no semidogs.}
\cpara{Says, with ``seems,'' that the mind prefers essences, and shows what an essence licenses: from Socrates's humanness you may infer his mortality without further tests.}

\cpara{Applies this to groups: polarization and a halo effect around a ``Favorite Thing Ever'' do not tell you whether a group is uncritical, whether its idea is true, or whether it will isolate and starve you.}
\cpara{Describes the argument that results: each side picks one characteristic from a checklist and declares the whole verdict.}
\cpara{Draws the conclusion of point one: judge the characteristics one at a time.}

\cpara{Applies ``Reversed Stupidity Is Not Intelligence'' (12 December 2007): a group's being a cult does not make its central idea false. ``Cultishness is a characteristic of groups more than hypotheses.''}

\cpara{The second error: the nervous asker wants reassurance, not an answer. This is the lesson of the first of the ``Two Cult Koans'' (21 December 2007), which the footnote cites. There the master tells a novice who fears his school is a cult: ``You came to me to seek reassurance. If you had been truly curious, not knowing one way or the other, you would have thought of ways to resolve your doubts.''}
\cpara{Restates the title claim of ``Every Cause Wants to Be a Cult'' and its image of effort against entropy, and applies it: a relieved ``It's not a cult!'' ends the effort.}

\cpara{Adds that a nervous member will refuse to see ordinary signs of cultishness, because any sign would imply membership of a cult. Examples of groups at risk: parties, startups, Mac and Linux users.}
\cpara{Announces the third mistake, with ``I strongly suspect'': the nervousness has the wrong source.}
\cpara{Asks why old groups with cult-like practices are called religions. The question is rhetorical; no group is named.}

\cpara{Compares the nervousness about cryonics with the calm about political rallies, where the same group errors occur. No evidence is given for the claim about ``most of the people who nervously ask.''}
\cpara{Grants one legitimate difference, a reputation for sleep deprivation, and notes that cryonicists lack it too.}

\clogic{The comparison leaves out what each asks of a newcomer. A rally asks for an evening. Cryonics asks for a payment that, as of 2011, ranged ``from \$28,000 to \$200,000'' in the United States and is ``often financed via life insurance,'' for storage ``in the hope that resurrection may be possible in the future'' (Wikipedia, ``Cryonics''). Nervousness before that commitment need not be fear of weirdness. The notes on ``Lonely Dissent'' raise the same difference against its comparison with skydiving.}
\cpara{The diagnosis, marked ``I suspect'': the nervousness is the fear of lonely dissent, the feeling of Asch's subjects facing a unanimous room.}
\cpara{Explains the earlier contrasts (old religions, political parties) by the diagnosis: ``cult'' is ``a label for something that seems weird.''}
\clogic{``That's why'' treats the previous paragraph's suspicion as established. No new evidence has been given for it.}

\cpara{Grants that weirdness justifies ``an extra burden of proof,'' then repeats the diagnosis without a hedge: the nervousness is ``the fear of believing something that will make your friends look at you really oddly.''}
\cpara{Mocks the view that odd belief itself causes the harms of cults, as if a ``Cult Fairy'' conferred them.}

\cpara{The key concession: ``socially unusual belief puts a group at risk for ingroup-outgroup thinking and evaporative cooling,'' and so does a lofty goal. Both are ``a risk factor, not a disease.''}
\cpara{Problem four: cults exploit the same fear of lonely dissent, by surrounding converts with agreement.}
\cpara{Observes that conformity keeps people out of cults and keeps members in: it ``glues you to wherever you are.''}
\cpara{Names the wish for a final answer ``need for closure,'' and says cults exploit that too.}

\cpara{Restates ``The Proper Use of Doubt'' (August 2007), which said that ``every doubt exists in order to annihilate some particular belief,'' and adds that some doubts take time to resolve and must be lived with.}
\cpara{Says that someone who cannot tell must choose under uncertainty, ``what decision theory is all about.'' The post does not say what such a choice would weigh.}

\cpara{Describes the caution the author approves of: people wary of AI ideas becoming a cult in future, through risk factors such as a ``Super Happy Agent.'' They ``can see at a glance'' that these ideas are not a cult now.}
\cpara{Says the author shares this worry and writes essays like this one to block it.}
\cpara{Adds that advice on how to think is itself a risk factor.}

\cpara{Contrasts the author's two causes. The author is asked ``Are you sure this isn't a cult?'' more often about powerful AIs than about probability theory, and says, with ``I don't know,'' that the difference is how weird each sounds.}

\clogic{By the post's own account, sounding weirder is itself a risk factor: ``socially unusual belief puts a group at risk for ingroup-outgroup thinking and evaporative cooling.'' Three paragraphs earlier the post also named a risk factor specific to the AI cause, the ``Super Happy Agent.'' Being asked more often about the weirder cause tracks risk factors the post names. It does not by itself show that the askers mistake weirdness for the disease.}

\cpara{Problem six: the question invites the ``plausible elaborate argument explaining Why This Is Not A Cult'' that an ``Evil Guru'' would give, and the author says this essay may be such reassurance. The post raises this risk itself. The Evil Guru repeats the first cult koan, whose master says: ``If I had been an evil man, I could have made you pay a hundred silver coins.''}
\cpara{Compares the author to the first dissenter in Asch's experiment, and calls the question ``a wrong question.''}
\cpara{The practical advice, in two sentences: look at the group's reasoning yourself, ``once you get rid of the fear of weirdness,'' and take responsibility for your own thinking.}

\cpara{Ends with the swordsman who does not glance away to see who is laughing, an image from the first cult koan (``You are like a swordsman who keeps glancing away to see if anyone might be laughing at him'').}

\clogic{The closing test sits uneasily with the essay's own warning that ``having a nice goal always puts you at risk of the happy death spiral.'' A member who knows ``what you're trying to do and why'' is the case the essay said was at risk. Knowing one's goal does not show whether a group serves it.}
